newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Warcrimes trial disrupted by Bosnia logistics.
newsitem.headline: Warcrimes trial disrupted by Bosnia logistics.

text.p: Proceedings at a U.N. war crimes trial in The Hague ground to an unscheduled halt on Thursday when logistics problems prevented witnesses from appearing via a live satellite link from Banja Luka in Bosnia.

Two witnesses, called to testify in defence of Dusan Tadic, a Bosnian Serb accused of killing, raping and torturing non-Serbs as part of an "ethnic cleansing" campaign in northwest Bosnia in the summer of 1992, were not immediately available to take the stand and give remote testimony.

Tadic's defence counsel has had problems getting witnesses to testify. Some are unwilling, others are afraid to travel to the U.N. criminal tribunal for former Yugoslavia in The Hague for fear they, too, might be arrested for war crimes.

To get around that, tribunal judges have given special permission for defence witnesses to testify via a live satellite link from Banja Luka, but transmission delays and poor sound quality clearly frustrate many in the court.
Logistics in the former war zone also make it difficult to get witnesses to Banja Luka at short notice.

Defence lawyer Michail Wladimiroff told the court from Bosnia that one of the two men unavailable on Thursday had already testified this week via satellite but was too far away to be recalled for cross-examination. Both were expected to appear when the trial resumes on Friday.
These "remote" witnesses testify from a small, dimly lit room in a secure United Nations building in Banja Luka.

Sitting at a desk in front of a large U.N. flag, and in the presence of representatives from the defence, prosecution and the tribunal's registry, they can follow the Hague court proceedings via headphones and a monitor.
In The Hague, the testimony is often garbled and disjointed, with long pauses for transmission and interpretation, making for laboured questioning and cross-examination.
The link, via the U.N's global satellite system, often crashes, leaving those in court staring at a blank monitor.
Judges have stressed that remote testimony is an exception and would not weigh as heavily as evidence given in court.
Earlier on Thursday, Tadic's sister-in-law told the court she saw him frequently in Prijedor at a time when he was accused of touring prison camps on an orgy of violence against Moslems.

Called as a defence alibi witness, Jelena Gajic, 39, sister of Tadic's wife Mira, said Tadic had visited her flat in Prijedor on May 23, 1992, the day before his mainly-Moslem home village of Kozarac, several kms away, was attacked by Serbs.
Speaking through an interpreter and via the satellite link, Gajic, a hospital anaesthetist, said Tadic had left Kozarac and was taking his family to Banja Luka -- 50 kms east of Prijedor.
She told the three judges that she had next seen her brother-in-law in mid-June, again in Prijedor.
"I saw him often after he'd moved back to Prijedor," she said. "He came to see how we were doing after all the turmoil."

Tadic's defence has called a number of alibi witnesses to testify to having seen or been with Tadic during the summer of 1992 when, the prosecution alleges, he was committing atrocities. Tadic denies the charges.

The trial, which began in May, is expected to end next month, with a verdict in the spring. The majority of the 75 suspects charged by the Hague tribunal, including former Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic and his army commander General Ratko Mladic, remain at liberty. One has died and seven are in tribunal custody.
